Hi Logan,

Thanks for taking this — Velotech is exploring a short pilot to validate inference cost reductions using batching, KV prefix caching, and quantization. A few details up front that will affect packaging:
- Estimated steady usage: ~10M tokens / month (mix of user prompts + assistant responses)
- Typical input sequence length: 80 tokens; output median: 130 tokens, 95th pct: 450 tokens
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 150ms for interactive flows (some non-interactive async batch ok)
- Model family: currently evaluating open Llama-family variants and an internal fine-tuned Llama-2.

What we're trying to understand: realistic downside/upside of int8/int4-like quantization on quality, expected per-token cost reduction from caching & batching for our distribution, and what a 1–3 month pilot packaging looks like (credits, discounts, scope). Hi Priya — great to meet you (virtually). Thanks for the concise rundown — that's very helpful.

Quick answers up front and then next steps:
- We can usually get 35–60% per-token compute reduction with int8 on Llama variants; int4 can push savings higher but quality impact is model- and prompt-dependent.
- KV/prefix caching combined with continuous batching tends to reduce token counts to service by ~20–40% for assistant-heavy workloads where prompts repeat or include long system prefixes.
- For your latency SLO (p95 <= 150ms) we'll likely recommend a hybrid config: smallish batching windows (8–12 tokens / concurrency-aware) + warmed-up KV pools for hot prefixes. That keeps tail latency predictable.

To put together a concrete pilot proposal I need two quick things from your side:
1) A sample of prompt/response pairs (anonymized) or length distribution export (CSV is fine).
2) Any regulatory constraints (data residency, logging retention limits) beyond the doc attached — call to confirm.

Hi Priya and Logan,

I put together some initial, conservative recommendations tailored to the distribution you described. See the short summary below — full notes attached (redwood_quant_batching_recs.pdf) and a scenario CSV (sample-budget-scenario.csv) that extrapolates cost at different commit/credit levels.

Summary recommendations (technical):
- Quantization: start with per-layer aware int8 (we have validated paths for Llama-family up to int8 across our runtime). Expect 35% compute reduction on average; quality regressions are rare but non-zero — run a 1000-sample eval set (we can help).
- Aggressive int4: only for non-critical pipelines / post-processed outputs. We recommend A/B gating + fallback to int8 on quality regressions.
- Batching: target an effective batch size of 6–10 for interactive flows; 12–24 for async/queued jobs. Use a dynamic timeout heuristic: 12–25ms window for interactive to balance latency and throughput.
- KV/prefix caching: enable per-account hot-key caching with an LRU TTL of 15–30 minutes. For your load shape this should reduce total token compute by ~18–30% depending on prompt repetition.
- Autoscale knobs: configure lane-based pools (low-latency lane pinned to smaller batch sizes, medium lane for cost-efficient throughput).

Operational caveats:
- Latency p95 sensitivity: at 95th+ token lengths (400–600 tokens) batching can increase p95 unless we pre-warm KV and reserve headroom for the low-latency lane. We'll include warm-up churn in the pilot plan.
- Eval & rollback: include a lightweight quality monitor tied to a 500-sample prompt set; auto-fallback to int8 if quality drift > 2% measured on key metrics.

Expected cost delta (illustrative):
- Baseline (no quant, minimal batching): $0.060 / 1k tokens
- With int8 + caching + tuned batching: $0.028–0.035 / 1k tokens (roughly 40–55% reduction)
